Painter and decorator by trade, tinkerer with automation tooling by habit. Based in Edmonton, Alberta — I run a hands-on residential painting and home renovation operation, with prep done properly, clean lines, and a finish that lasts.

The same instinct that keeps a paint edge sharp keeps the paperwork tidy: this site doubles as the home of the small tools and checklists I built to stop small jobs turning into big ones. What works on real job sites ends up shared here.

Text is the fastest way to reach me — fire off an enquiry any time, or email first if you prefer. Happy to quote: see the services below, or send over a few photos of the space and I'll come back with a plan and a number.
How do I get a quote?

Message me on Facebook, text, or use the quote form on this page. Send photos of the space, what you want painted, and your timeline. I follow up with a free quote and next steps. Quotes are in writing, so there's a record of exactly what's included.
How long does a job take?
A single room is usually 1 to 2 days. A full interior is usually 3 to 7 days depending on size, prep, and drying time. You get a clear timeline before work starts.
Do you move furniture and protect my home?
Yes. Furniture is moved and covered, floors are protected, trim is taped and masked, and drop cloths are used throughout. Cleanup is daily, with a final walkthrough with you.
What paint do you use?

Quality, low-odor paints suited for the surface. Tell me if you have kids, pets, or sensitivities and I'll pick the right product. If you already have a color, send it and I'll match it. For low-odour interior work I'll suggest zero-VOC options, which is worth it in an Edmonton winter when windows stay shut.
Do you supply the paint or do I?
Either works. I can price the job with materials included (I use trade-grade lines I trust) or work on labour-only with your paint. Supplies are a genuine choice, not an upsell.
Do you help with color?
Yes. I can help you narrow down 2 to 3 colors that work with your lighting and flooring, and test swatches on the wall before we commit.
Do you clean up after?
Yes. Daily cleanup, plus a full final cleanup. Paint cans, tape, and drop cloths are removed. You come home to a finished room, not a job site.
Can you fix drywall before painting?
Yes — patching, filling nail pops, taping minor cracks and sanding are standard prep in my quotes. Larger drywall sections I'll flag honestly if a drywall specialist makes more sense.
What areas do you serve?

Yes — I'm based in west-central Edmonton and regularly work in St. Albert, Sherwood Park, Spruce Grove, Stony Plain, Leduc, Beaumont and Fort Saskatchewan. Travel within the Edmonton metro is included in quotes.
How far ahead should I book?
Interior work can often start within a couple of weeks. Exterior work in Edmonton is weather-dependent — May through September fills up first, so book exterior repaints ahead of the season.
How do I book?
Message me to hold your dates. Scope, color, timeline, and quote are confirmed in writing before work starts.

How to prep walls before painting: Edmonton interior checklist
DRAFT — owner review before publishing: A wall-prep checklist for Edmonton interior painting — clearing, repairs, filling, sanding and cutting-in, in the order prep actually happens on site.

A fresh coat of paint is only as good as what's underneath it. On interior jobs in Edmonton, prep is where most of the time on site goes — and the checklist below is roughly the order the work happens in a real room.

Clear the room first. Furniture out (or pushed to the centre and sheeted), outlet covers and switch plates off, window hardware and anything hanging on the walls down. Bagging hardware and labelling the bags saves a lot of head-scratching at reassembly time.

Wall prep comes next. Scuff-sand shiny spots and any glossy paint where new paint needs to grip, fill nail holes and small dings with filler, and let it dry properly before a light second sand. Greasy areas — kitchen walls especially — get washed down so paint doesn't lift later.

Nail pops, loose drywall tape and crumbly filler get cut back and redone rather than painted over; a patched spot that flashes through a finished coat means redoing the whole wall. Where patches are bigger, spotting primer on the repairs stops them from showing as dull or shiny patches under the finish coat.
Dust and cutting-in are the last prep steps before paint: floors sheeted, vacuum done, then a careful cut-in line along ceilings, trim and corners so the roller work stays in the middle of the wall.
That's the sequence that keeps an interior job tidy and makes the finish last — and it's why a quote should mention prep hours, not just coats of paint.
Home renovation checklist: what order should the work be done in?
DRAFT — owner review before publishing: The order renovation work follows — dusty before clean, wet before dry, rough before finish — and why the sequence matters more than the calendar.

Homeowners often ask what order a renovation should happen in — and the honest answer is that the sequence exists to stop finished work from getting wrecked by work that comes later. Here's the order small renovation jobs around Edmonton typically follow.

Structural and layout work comes first: anything touching framing, openings or plumbing rough-in happens before anything cosmetic. There's no point taping and mudding drywall if a wall is about to move.

Then the "wet and dusty" trades, roughly in this order: HVAC and plumbing rough-in, electrical rough-in, insulation, drywall hang and tape, then sanding. Sanding drywall dust gets everywhere, so flooring and anything finished stays out until the dust work is done.

After dust comes moisture-prone work: paint and cabinet-adjacent finishes. On repaint-and-refresh jobs we're often called in at this stage — repairs, prep and finishing work once the dusty phases are finished.

Then flooring goes in, followed by trim, doors and fixture setting. Flooring before trim lets the trim sit down onto the finished floor for a clean line; installing trim first usually means scribing and fudging later.
Fixtures, hardware and punch-list last. Switch plates, faucet handles, doorstops and the little touch-ups get finished once everything heavy is out of the way.

The rule of thumb: dusty before clean, wet before dry, rough before finish. If a quote has painting scheduled before flooring, ask why — getting the order right is most of what keeps a reno on schedule.
When is the best time to paint a house exterior in Alberta?
DRAFT — owner review before publishing: Alberta's exterior painting window explained — surface temperature, overnight lows, and why June-to-early-September is the dependable range.

Alberta weather makes exterior painting a seasonal question — paint needs the right surface temperature and enough curing time before frost, and Edmonton doesn't offer a huge window. Here's roughly how the season plays out.

Late spring through early fall is the workable window. The general rule most paints quote is surface (not just air) temperatures above about 10°C, with temperatures staying in range long enough for the coat to cure — overnight lows matter as much as afternoon highs.

Early summer is the dependable sweet spot: long daylight hours, warm surfaces, and no morning dew issues. Late August and September can also be very good painting weather — the catch is how fast the season can end, because the first hard frost can arrive earlier than expected.

Spring is the gamble. May snowfall isn't unusual on the prairies, and surfaces on the north side of a house can stay cold well into the day even when the afternoon feels fine. Shady walls need a temperature check before paint goes on, not after.

Even within a good day, the window matters: morning dew and evening temperature drops shrink the usable hours at the edges of the season. Exterior jobs are scheduled around the forecast, not around the calendar.

Practical answer: for exterior painting in Alberta, aim for June through early September, watch overnight lows, and treat late-season dates as weather-permitting. Planning an exterior job? Booking early-summer dates is the safest bet.
